hero.lead: A defined process for reading liquidity, structure and execution — written down, tested against data, and taught step by step.
hero.sceneDescription: A scroll-driven diagram walking through one setup: market context, liquidity, sweep, market structure shift, fair value gap, then entry with a defined stop and target.

system.label: System

system.title: A setup is not the system
system.lead: A setup is one stage inside a closed process. What produces a result is the order of the stages, not an isolated pattern.
system.loopTitle: Data changes how the market is read
system.loopBody: The output of the last stage is the input to the first. That is what makes this a system rather than a checklist: review and data do not end the process, they decide what counts as context next time.

market.label: Market
market.question: What is actually in front of me?
market.body: The market produces movement all day. Most of it is information about positioning, not an opportunity. The first discipline is refusing to treat every move as a signal.

context.label: Context
context.question: Does this environment suit the setup at all?
context.body: Session, higher-timeframe direction, the range in force, the levels that matter. Context decides whether a setup is worth looking for, before any entry is considered.

liquidity.label: Liquidity
liquidity.question: Where are the resting orders?
liquidity.body: Price travels toward places where orders are parked. Equal highs and lows are obvious to everyone, which is exactly what makes them a destination rather than a barrier.

structure.label: Structure
structure.question: Has direction actually changed?
structure.body: A shift is a rule, not an impression. Structure gives the change a definition that can be checked afterwards, and disagreed with.

setup.label: Setup
setup.question: Does this match something written down?
setup.body: Context, liquidity and structure together produce a candidate, not a signal. A setup is a specification with conditions, and the Setup Lab is where it becomes a testable hypothesis.

execution.label: Execution
execution.question: What exactly triggers the decision?
execution.body: Entry, invalidation and target are defined before risk is taken. Entry is a decision point. It is not an outcome, and a trade that moved in your favour was not correct for that reason.

risk.label: Risk
risk.question: What is this allowed to cost?
risk.body: Invalidation is chosen from structure, and size follows from the invalidation. Risk is decided first because it is the only part of a trade fully under control.

review.label: Review
review.question: Was the process followed?
review.body: That question is separate from whether the trade won. A rule followed on a loser is a good trade; a rule broken on a winner is the expensive one.

data.label: Data
data.question: What do the records say?
data.body: Individual trades are anecdotes. Enough of them, recorded the same way, and the process starts describing its own behaviour, which is the only honest basis for changing it.

market.definition: The continuous stream of price and participation, before any interpretation is applied to it.

context.definition: The conditions surrounding a possible trade: session, higher-timeframe direction, range and volatility.

liquidity.definition: Areas where resting orders accumulate, which price tends to move toward rather than away from.

structure.definition: The sequence of swing highs and lows that describes direction in a way that can be checked.

setup.definition: A written specification of conditions that together identify a candidate trade.

execution.definition: Opening a defined position once its trigger conditions are met.

risk.definition: The predetermined amount a trade is allowed to cost, decided before entry.

review.definition: Assessment of whether the process was followed, kept separate from whether the trade profited.

data.definition: Accumulated trade records treated as a sample, used to describe the process rather than to justify it.

equalHighs.definition: Two or more highs at effectively the same price, marking a pool of resting orders above them.

equalLows.definition: Two or more lows at effectively the same price, marking a pool of resting orders below them.

sweep.definition: Price trading through a liquidity level and rejecting, taking the orders resting there.

bos.definition: Price closing beyond a prior swing point in the direction of the existing trend.

mss.definition: A break of structure against the prevailing direction, defining a change rather than a continuation.

displacement.definition: An impulsive move that leaves imbalance behind, separating intent from ordinary movement.

fvg.definition: The unfilled price range left behind by an impulsive move, often used as a location to act from.

entry.definition: The specific price and condition at which a position is opened.

invalidation.definition: The price at which the reason for the trade no longer holds.

positionSize.definition: The quantity chosen so that reaching invalidation costs the predetermined amount.

lab.title: A library of written hypotheses
lab.lead: Each setup is a specification: the conditions that have to hold, and the point at which it is wrong. None of them carry performance figures, because none of them have been tested yet.

evidence.conceptual: Conceptual. A written specification, not yet tested against data.
evidence.demo: Demo data. Placeholder values standing in for a source that is not connected.
evidence.insufficient: Insufficient sample. Tested, but below the minimum for any claim.

liquidity-sweep-reversal.title: Liquidity sweep reversal
liquidity-sweep-reversal.purpose: A level everyone can see is taken, and the move that follows breaks structure in the opposite direction.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.context: A market that has been trending into an obvious high or low, with enough session time left for a reaction to develop.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.liquidity: A clear pool: equal highs, a prior session high, or a swing everybody is watching. The more obvious it is, the better it works as a destination.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.structure: Prior swing structure must be intact before the sweep, so the break afterwards is measurable rather than a matter of opinion.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.trigger: Price trades through the level and closes back inside, then displaces through the opposing swing point. Both halves are required.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.entry: The imbalance left by the displacement, entered on the retracement into it rather than chased at the break.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.invalidation: Above the sweep high, or below the sweep low. If price reclaims the level the reading was wrong, and nothing about it needs reinterpreting.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.risk: Sized so that reaching invalidation costs the predetermined amount. The distance is defined by the sweep, never by a preferred position size.
liquidity-sweep-reversal.review: Was the level genuinely obvious beforehand, or obvious only afterwards? That question separates this setup from hindsight.

session-open-displacement.title: Session open displacement
session-open-displacement.purpose: The first decisive move after a session opens, taken at the imbalance it leaves behind.
session-open-displacement.context: The opening window of a session with real participation. Outside that window the same pattern has a different meaning.
session-open-displacement.liquidity: Liquidity built during the quiet period before the open, in the range that formed while nothing was trading.
session-open-displacement.structure: No structural read is required before the open. The displacement itself creates the structure this setup uses.
session-open-displacement.trigger: An impulsive move away from the pre-open range that leaves an unfilled gap. Movement without imbalance does not qualify.
session-open-displacement.entry: The gap, on the first return into it. If price does not return there is no trade, and waiting is the setup working correctly.
session-open-displacement.invalidation: The far side of the gap. A fill means the imbalance is resolved and the reason for the location is gone.
session-open-displacement.risk: Tighter than most setups because the invalidation is close, which raises position size. Size still follows the stop, never the other way round.
session-open-displacement.review: Did the move actually displace, or was it a wide range bar in slow conditions? Recording that distinction is what makes the sample usable later.

equal-highs-draw.title: Equal highs as a draw
equal-highs-draw.purpose: Two highs at the same price are not resistance. They are a destination.
equal-highs-draw.context: A range or a slow trend where price has printed the same high more than once without breaking away.
equal-highs-draw.liquidity: The equal highs themselves. Orders rest above them, which is what gives price a reason to travel there.
equal-highs-draw.structure: Structure matters only as confirmation that the market is not already in a decisive move away from the level.
equal-highs-draw.trigger: Price beginning to move toward the level rather than away from it, in a session with enough time left to reach it.
equal-highs-draw.entry: Positional, into the draw. This is a directional bias rather than a precise trigger, and it is described that way on purpose.
equal-highs-draw.invalidation: A close beyond the opposite side of the range. At that point the equal highs are no longer the nearest draw.
equal-highs-draw.risk: Wider stop, smaller size. The trade-off is explicit: a positional idea cannot be given an intraday stop and still make sense.
equal-highs-draw.review: Did price reach the level at all? A setup that identifies a destination is judged on whether the destination was reached, not on the entry.

structure-shift-continuation.title: Structure shift continuation
structure-shift-continuation.purpose: A break in the direction of the existing trend, read as continuation rather than reversal.
structure-shift-continuation.context: An established trend with at least two confirmed swings in the same direction. Without that, the break has nothing to continue.
structure-shift-continuation.liquidity: Liquidity resting beneath the most recent higher low, or above the most recent lower high, in the pullback that precedes the break.
structure-shift-continuation.structure: The defining element. A break of structure in the trend direction, closed rather than wicked, measured against a swing that was there beforehand.
structure-shift-continuation.trigger: The close beyond the prior swing point, with the pullback that preceded it still intact.
structure-shift-continuation.entry: The retracement toward the broken level, which is now the nearest reference rather than a barrier.
structure-shift-continuation.invalidation: Beneath the low that produced the break. Losing it means the trend read is no longer supported by structure.
structure-shift-continuation.risk: Straightforward, because the invalidation is structural and does not need to be chosen. That is the argument for this setup over a discretionary entry.
structure-shift-continuation.review: Was the trend real at the point of entry, or two swings inside a range? Most losses on this setup are context failures, not trigger failures.

range-to-expansion.title: Range to expansion
range-to-expansion.purpose: A defined range, then the move that leaves it. The setup is the transition, not the range.
range-to-expansion.context: An extended balanced period, usually across a quiet session, with a range whose edges have been respected more than once.
range-to-expansion.liquidity: Both edges of the range hold liquidity. Which side is taken first is information, not noise.
range-to-expansion.structure: Inside the range, structure is meaningless. It becomes readable only once one side is left behind.
range-to-expansion.trigger: A decisive move out of the range that does not immediately return: displacement away from balance rather than another test of an edge.
range-to-expansion.entry: On the first retracement toward the range edge that was broken, treating it as the new reference.
range-to-expansion.invalidation: A return inside the range. If balance is restored the expansion did not happen and the premise is void.
range-to-expansion.risk: Position sizing is the hard part here. The stop is far by construction, so this setup is often correct and still unsuitable for the account.
range-to-expansion.review: How long was the range, and did that predict anything about the move? This is the setup where recording the context pays for itself.

academy.lead: Eight lessons, in order. Each one teaches a concept the rest of this site already uses, shows it on a chart, and points at the setups built from it. Free, no account, nothing to buy.

academy.endOfPath: That is the last lesson in this path.

market-and-noise.title: The market and the noise
market-and-noise.summary: Most of what price does is not a signal. The first skill is telling the difference.
market-and-noise.explain: A market produces movement continuously, and almost none of it is an opportunity. Movement is information about positioning: who had to buy, who had to sell, and where. Treating every move as a signal is not aggression, it is a category error — it mistakes activity for meaning. Everything else in this academy exists to narrow attention down to the small number of moments that carry information you can act on.
market-and-noise.visualize: On the chart the opening stretch is deliberately unremarkable: price moves, ranges, moves back. Nothing about it says what to do. That is the honest picture of most of a session, and a method that cannot sit through it is not a method.
market-and-noise.apply: Before looking for an entry, name the environment. Which session is this, what has price done today, and is there a reason to expect participation? If the answer is that nothing is happening, the correct action is to do nothing, and recording that is as much a decision as taking a trade.
market-and-noise.check: Look at any chart from the last week and mark the moves you would have called signals at the time. Then mark which ones you could have defined by a rule beforehand. The gap between those two counts is the problem this academy is about.
takeaways: Movement is not opportunity.
Context decides whether a setup is worth looking for.
Doing nothing is a decision that should be recorded.

market-structure.title: Market structure
market-structure.summary: Direction becomes checkable when highs and lows are read as a sequence rather than a feeling.
market-structure.explain: Structure is the sequence of swing highs and lows, and its value is that it turns direction into something you can be wrong about. A trend is not an impression, it is a series of higher highs and higher lows that either continues or does not. A break of structure is price closing beyond a prior swing in the direction of the trend. A market structure shift is a break against it, and that is the one that defines a change rather than a continuation.
market-structure.visualize: In the sequence you can see a run of higher highs, a pullback that sets a swing low, and then a decisive move through that low. The break is measurable because the low existed beforehand and can be pointed at.
market-structure.apply: Mark the most recent swing high and swing low before you form any opinion. If you cannot mark them, there is no structure to trade, and that is itself an answer. Once marked, a shift is either present or absent — no interpretation required.
market-structure.check: On a chart you have not seen, mark the last three swing points and state which direction structure says the market is in. Then check whether the following move agreed. The point is not to be right; it is to have made a claim that could be checked.
takeaways: Structure turns direction into a rule instead of an impression.
A break with the trend continues it; a break against it defines a change.
If the swing points cannot be marked, there is nothing to read.

liquidity.title: Liquidity
liquidity.summary: Price travels toward the places where orders are waiting, not away from them.
liquidity.explain: Liquidity is where resting orders accumulate: above obvious highs, below obvious lows, around levels everyone can see. This is the idea that most reverses the beginner's intuition. An obvious level is not a wall that stops price — it is a reason for price to go there, because that is where the orders that need filling are sitting. Equal highs are not resistance. They are a destination.
liquidity.visualize: The chart shows a level formed by highs at effectively the same price, and then price reaching through it and rejecting. The reach is not a failure of the level; it is the level doing what it was always going to do.
liquidity.apply: Before deciding direction, ask which side is more obvious to everyone else. That side is the more likely draw. This does not tell you to trade it — it tells you where price is being pulled while you are deciding.
liquidity.check: Find two highs at the same price on any chart. Did price eventually trade through them? Note how long it took. The waiting is usually the difficult part, not the recognition.
takeaways: Obvious levels attract price rather than repelling it.
Equal highs and lows mark pools of resting orders.
A sweep is the level working, not the level failing.

displacement-and-imbalance.title: Displacement and imbalance
displacement-and-imbalance.summary: Some moves leave a gap behind. That gap is what makes the location specific.
displacement-and-imbalance.explain: Displacement is an impulsive move that separates intent from ordinary movement. Its useful by-product is imbalance: when price moves fast enough, it leaves a range where trading was one-sided, visible as an unfilled gap between one candle's low and another's high. That gap is a fair value gap, and it matters because it converts a direction into a location. Without it you know which way to look; with it you know where to act.
displacement-and-imbalance.visualize: Look at the steep leg in the sequence. The move is fast, the bodies are large, and the space it leaves is not revisited immediately. That untouched space is the imbalance.
displacement-and-imbalance.apply: Use the gap as the place to act from, on the retracement into it, rather than chasing the break. If price never returns, there is no trade — and that is the setup working correctly, not a missed opportunity.
displacement-and-imbalance.check: Find an impulsive move on any chart and check whether it left a gap. Then check whether price returned to it. Both answers are informative; the second one is the one traders skip.
takeaways: Displacement separates intent from ordinary movement.
The imbalance it leaves converts direction into a location.
No return to the gap means no trade.

building-a-setup.title: Building a setup
building-a-setup.summary: A setup is a written specification with conditions, not a pattern you recognise.
building-a-setup.explain: Context, liquidity and structure together produce a candidate. Alone, none of them is a reason to act: a level without structure is a guess, and structure without context is a rule applied in the wrong environment. A setup is the written statement of which conditions must hold together, and — just as importantly — the point at which it is no longer valid. If it cannot be written down before the session, it is not a setup, it is a memory of one.
building-a-setup.visualize: The sequence shows the conditions arriving in order: a level, a sweep of it, a structural break, and the imbalance left behind. The setup is the conjunction, not any single element.
building-a-setup.apply: Write the conditions as a list, then look for that list. The discipline is in the order: the specification comes first, and the chart is checked against it. Reversing that produces a setup that always seems to have been present.
building-a-setup.check: Take a trade you took recently and try to write its conditions as a specification. If you cannot state what would have made it invalid, it was not a setup.
takeaways: A setup is a conjunction of conditions, never one pattern.
It must be writable before the session, not after the move.
If invalidation cannot be stated, there is no specification.

execution.title: Execution
execution.summary: Entry is a decision point. It is not an outcome, and a profitable trade was not therefore correct.
execution.explain: Execution is the moment analysis becomes a position. The entry is defined by the trigger condition, not by conviction, and it is decided before risk is taken along with the invalidation and the target. The distinction that matters most here is between decision and outcome: a trade that moved in your favour was not correct for that reason, and one that did not was not therefore wrong. Judging execution by results teaches the wrong lesson at exactly the moment it feels most convincing.
execution.visualize: The chart shows the entry level marked against the imbalance, with the invalidation above and the target below. All three exist before anything happens.
execution.apply: Define entry, invalidation and target before placing the order. If any of the three cannot be specified, the trade is not ready — and reducing size does not fix a missing invalidation.
execution.check: Look at your last five trades and check whether entry, stop and target were all defined before entry. The ones where they were not are the ones worth reviewing first.
takeaways: Entry is defined by a trigger, not by conviction.
All three levels exist before risk is taken.
A winning trade is not evidence that the decision was correct.

risk.title: Risk
risk.summary: Invalidation comes from structure. Size comes from invalidation. Never the other way round.
risk.explain: Risk is the one part of a trade fully under control, which is why it is decided first. Invalidation is the price at which the reason for the trade no longer holds, and it is chosen from structure rather than from a comfortable distance. Position size then follows arithmetically: the quantity that makes reaching invalidation cost the predetermined amount. Choosing size first and then placing a stop where that size allows is the most common way a defensible idea becomes an indefensible trade.
risk.visualize: On the chart, invalidation sits above the sweep and the target below the displacement. The distance between them is a property of the market's structure, not of what would be convenient.
risk.apply: Work in this order every time: find invalidation from structure, decide what the trade may cost, then compute size. If the resulting size is uncomfortably small, the honest conclusion is that this setup does not suit this account right now.
risk.check: Take a setup you like and compute the size for a fixed risk amount. If the number surprises you, that surprise is the information.
takeaways: Risk is decided before entry because it is the only controllable part.
Invalidation is structural, not a preferred distance.
Size follows the stop; reversing the order breaks the logic.

review-and-data.title: Review and data
review-and-data.summary: Review asks whether the process was followed. That is a separate question from whether it won.
review-and-data.explain: A trade produces two independent facts: whether the rule was followed, and whether the outcome was positive. Conflating them is how a lucky break becomes a habit and a disciplined loss becomes a doubt. Review separates them. Once enough trades are recorded the same way, the records stop being anecdotes and start describing the process itself — and that description is the only honest basis for changing it. This is where the loop closes: data changes what counts as context next time.
review-and-data.visualize: The final frame shows the whole sequence at once. Individually the elements were moments; together they are a process that can be repeated and therefore measured.
review-and-data.apply: After each trade, record the specification it matched and whether it was followed, separately from the result. Do not adjust rules on single outcomes — a sample of one describes nothing.
review-and-data.check: Classify your last ten trades as rule-followed or not, ignoring profit entirely. The distribution usually explains more than the profit and loss does.
takeaways: Following the rule and winning are independent facts.
A rule followed on a loss is a good trade.
One trade is an anecdote; the sample is the evidence.
